title: A Star from Jacob: Balaam's Final Oracles
summary: Balaam abandons his usual divination, and the Spirit of God comes upon him as he sees Israel camped tribe by tribe. He blesses Israel a third time, praising its tents and repeating the blessing given to Abraham. Balak angrily dismisses him, but before leaving Balaam delivers a fourth oracle about a star and a scepter that will rise from Israel to crush Moab and conquer Edom, followed by brief oracles about Amalek, the Kenites, and ships from Cyprus.
story: This chapter brings the Balaam story to its climax. Balak has brought Balaam to a third height and built seven altars at each place, and twice already his curse has become a blessing. Now the tone changes. Balaam no longer goes off to seek omens; he simply looks at Israel, and the Spirit of God comes on him. His third oracle is the fullest blessing yet, and his fourth, spoken without being asked, looks far beyond the moment to a future king of Israel. The Balaam story thus ties together two great lines of promise: God's pledge to bless Abraham's descendants (Genesis 12:3) and the hope of a ruler from Judah whom the nations will obey (Genesis 49:10). The next chapter will turn back to Israel's own failures, but this chapter has already shown that God's purposes for his people rest on his word, not theirs.
historical:
The oracles mention real peoples of the region. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, Edom and Seir to the south, and Amalek was a nomadic people of the southern desert who had attacked Israel after the exodus (Exodus 17:8-16). The Kenites were a clan associated with Moses' father-in-law (Judges 1:16) who lived among or near Israel. Asshur is Assyria, the Mesopotamian empire that would dominate the region in the ninth to seventh centuries BC. The coasts of Cyprus (Hebrew Kittim, originally a name for Cyprus and later used more broadly for peoples from the west across the sea) appear in the final oracle. The phrase sons of Sheth in verse 17 is obscure; it may refer to a people or tribe of the region, but its identification is uncertain.

Later Israelite history fulfilled parts of the fourth oracle. Saul fought the Amalekites and their king Agag (1 Samuel 15), which gives the reference to Agag in verse 7 its point, and David subdued both Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 14). Scholars who date the oracles late see these references as written with that history in view; those who accept their early setting read them as genuine prediction. Either way, Jewish interpreters in the Second Temple period read the star oracle as pointing to a future messianic ruler. The Dead Sea Scrolls quote it in that sense, and in AD 132 the leader of the second Jewish revolt against Rome, Simon bar Kosiba, was hailed as Bar Kokhba, son of the star, in apparent reference to this verse.
cultural:
Verse 1 notes that Balaam did not resort to sorcery as before. The Hebrew word (nachash) refers to omen-reading, the practice he had apparently been using when he went off alone on the heights. Now he simply looks and speaks. The opening lines of both oracles in this chapter (verses 3 and 4, 15 and 16) use the language of prophetic inspiration: the man whose eyes are open, who hears the words of God and sees a vision from the Almighty. The word translated prophecy (ne'um) is the same term used in the formula declares the LORD throughout the prophets.

The images of verses 5 to 7 come from the life of a people in a dry land. Tents spread out like palm groves and gardens by a stream; water flows from buckets; aloes and cedars grow beside the waters. To a people who had spent forty years in the wilderness, these pictures of abundant water promised settled prosperity. The star and scepter in verse 17 were both royal symbols in the ancient Near East: kings were compared to stars, and a scepter was the staff that marked a ruler's authority.
literary: The chapter has two main oracles in parallel form, each with an elaborate introduction (verses 3 to 4 and 15 to 16), followed by three short sayings about other nations (20 to 24). The introductions build in the second oracle by adding who has knowledge from the Most High. The third oracle echoes two blessings from Genesis: “He crouches, he lies down like a lion” recalls Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9), and “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you” recalls God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and Isaac's blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27:29). Balaam's speeches have become a summary of Genesis's promises. The fourth oracle opens with a striking pair of lines, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near”, which signals that its subject lies in the distant future.

outline.t: Balaam gives up sorcery and the Spirit comes upon him
The third oracle: how lovely are your tents
The fourth oracle: a star and a scepter
Oracles on Amalek, the Kenites, and Asshur

doctrines.note: The star and scepter oracle is one of the Old Testament's early hints of a coming royal ruler from Israel. It was read in Jewish and Christian tradition as pointing to the Messiah, and it builds on the promise of a ruler from Judah in Genesis 49:10.

The Spirit of God comes upon Balaam, an outsider with mixed motives, enabling him to speak God's word. The Spirit's gift of prophecy is God's sovereign act and is not a certificate of the speaker's character.

Balaam's words in verse 9 echo the blessing of Genesis 12:3, in wording closest to Isaac's blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27:29). God's covenant with Abraham is still the governing reality of Israel's history, even after a generation of rebellion.

words.note: Kokhav, star. In the ancient Near East kings and divine beings were often associated with stars. Here the star from Jacob is a future ruler, paired in parallel with the scepter, and the image later fed Jewish and Christian messianic hope.

Shevet, scepter or rod, also the word for tribe. As a scepter it is the symbol of royal rule. Genesis 49:10 uses the same word in saying that the scepter will not depart from Judah, and this oracle develops that promise.

Ne'um, utterance or oracle, the solemn word that introduces inspired speech. Nearly everywhere else it is used of the LORD's own declarations through his prophets. Its use for Balaam signals that God is speaking through him.

Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The Spirit of God coming on a person is a recurring Old Testament way of describing divine empowerment for a task, as later with the judges and with Saul. Here it marks the difference between Balaam's earlier omen-seeking and true prophecy.

christ: The fourth oracle stands behind the church's reading of Jesus as the royal ruler promised to Israel. “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” was read messianically in Judaism before Jesus, and the early church inherited that reading. Matthew's account of the magi following a star to the one born king of the Jews (Matthew 2:1-2) does not quote Numbers 24, but many interpreters have seen an echo of it, especially since the magi, like Balaam, are wise men from the east. In Revelation 22:16 Jesus calls himself the bright morning star and the root and descendant of David. Historically, the oracle's promises about Moab and Edom first found fulfillment in David, and Christians read David's kingdom as a pattern of the greater reign of David's son. The link between this oracle and Jesus is one of the more direct messianic lines in the Pentateuch, though the oracle itself does not describe how the ruler will come.

hard.q: How could a pagan diviner who later led Israel into sin speak true prophecy?
hard.a:
The Bible is clear that Balaam was not a faithful servant of God. Numbers 31:16 blames his advice for Israel's sin at Peor, and the New Testament remembers him for greed and for teaching others to stumble (2 Peter 2:15; Revelation 2:14). Yet in this chapter the Spirit of God comes upon him and he speaks words the rest of Scripture treats as true. Interpreters respond that the power of the prophecy lies in the God who gives it, not in the prophet. God can speak through an unwilling or unworthy speaker, as he made Balaam's donkey speak, and Scripture elsewhere records God's word coming through unlikely people (Caiaphas's words in John 11:49-52 are often compared).

The story also carries a warning. Balaam had words from God and even a vision of the future, but that did not make his heart right. Jesus warns that on the last day some will say they prophesied in his name and yet were never known by him (Matthew 7:22-23). Gifts and faithfulness are not the same thing.

questions: Balaam saw God's future for Israel clearly and still did not share in it. What is the difference between knowing true things about God and belonging to him?
Balak tried to buy a curse and received a blessing instead. How have you seen God turn something intended for harm into good, in Scripture or in your own life?
The star oracle speaks of a ruler seen from far off. How does the hope of a king who is coming but not yet here shape the way you live now?
